title: Intervals, subnets and bit tricks: concepts
seriesDescription: Shortest paths, union-find, tries, bits and CIDR, DP, greedy, backtracking and mock-interview habits, in pseudocode. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Merge intervals, meeting rooms, insert interval, CIDR and subnet arithmetic, popcount, n & (n-1) and XOR identities, without language-specific code.
source: LeetCode Merge Intervals, Meeting Rooms I/II, Insert Interval, Single Number, Counting Bits, Non-overlapping Intervals; RFC 4632; RFC 3021

questions.prompt: Merge the closed intervals [1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18], [17,20]. How many intervals are in the merged result?
Meetings are [1,4], [2,5], [3,6], [7,9]. What is the minimum number of rooms needed?
questions.explanation: At time 3 the first three meetings overlap (1-4, 2-5, 3-6), so 3 rooms are required; [7,9] can reuse a freed room. The answer is the maximum overlap depth.

questions.prompt: How many usable host addresses does a /26 IPv4 subnet have (excluding network and broadcast addresses)?
questions.explanation: 32 - 26 = 6 host bits, 2^6 = 64 addresses, minus network and broadcast = 62. (A /31 point-to-point link is a special case under RFC 3021.)

questions.prompt: How many /24 subnets fit inside one /16 block?
questions.explanation: A /24 has 8 more network bits than a /16, so the /16 splits into 2^8 = 256 subnets of /24. Each /24 holds 256 addresses, and 256 * 256 = 65,536 = 2^16.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum number of intervals to remove from [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4],[1,3]] so that the rest do not overlap (touching at an endpoint is allowed)?
questions.explanation: Remove [1,3]; the others touch only at endpoints. The greedy sorts by end time, keeps an interval whenever it starts at or after the last kept end, and counts the rest: n minus the maximum non-overlapping set, O(n log n).

questions.prompt: In 32-bit two's complement, what is the value of 12 & -12?
questions.explanation: 12 is 1100 and -12 is ...110100, so the AND leaves only the lowest set bit, 0100 = 4. The expression n & -n isolates that bit and drives Fenwick tree indexing.

questions.prompt: 1000 in binary is 1111101000. How many bits are set to 1?
questions.explanation: Ones in 1111101000: five in a row plus one more = 6. Brian Kernighan's n &= n - 1 loop would iterate exactly 6 times.

questions.prompt: What must you do to the interval list before the single-pass merge loop works?
questions.explanation: Sort by start (O(n log n)), then sweep in O(n), extending the last output interval or starting a new one.

options.text: Sort the intervals by start time.
options.why: Correct: with starts in order, only the last output interval can overlap the next one.

options.text: Sort by end time, then compare each interval with the first one in the output.
options.why: Sorting by end does not keep overlapping intervals adjacent in the way the sweep needs.

options.text: Build a hash set of all start times and look up each end.
options.why: A set of starts cannot tell you which intervals overlap.

options.text: Nothing, because the loop compares every pair of intervals anyway.
options.why: A single pass compares neighbours only, so the order must be established first.

questions.prompt: For a positive integer n, what does the expression (n & (n - 1)) == 0 test?
questions.explanation: Guard n > 0 because 0 & -1 == 0 would wrongly pass. The same n & (n-1) step removes the lowest set bit, which powers popcount.

options.text: That n is even, because the lowest bit of n is 0.
options.why: Even numbers like 6 give 6 & 5 = 4, which is not zero.

options.text: That n is a power of two, because n has exactly one set bit.
options.why: Correct: subtracting 1 flips the lone set bit and everything below it, so the AND is zero.

options.text: That n has exactly two set bits, one removed by the subtraction.
options.why: Two set bits leave one bit behind after the AND, so the result is non-zero.

options.text: That n is a multiple of 10, since n - 1 ends in 9.
options.why: Binary operations know nothing about decimal digits.

questions.prompt: What is the broadcast address of the subnet 192.168.10.77/26?
questions.explanation: Block size = 2^(32 - 26) = 64, so blocks start at 0, 64, 128, 192. The block containing .77 is .64 to .127, with usable hosts .65 to .126.

options.why: Correct: /26 blocks are 64 wide; 77 lies in 64-127, and the last address of the block is the broadcast.
That is the broadcast of the whole /24, not of the /26 block containing .77.
That is the network address (first address) of the block.
That is the last usable host; the broadcast is one higher.

questions.prompt: You must insert one new interval into a sorted list of non-overlapping intervals.
questions.explanation: Add intervals ending before the new one, merge all that overlap by min of starts and max of ends, then append the rest.
questions.assertion: Insert Interval can be solved in O(n) time without sorting again.
questions.reason: The existing list is already sorted and non-overlapping, so one left-to-right pass (before, overlapping, after) is enough.

whys.a: Right: the sorted, disjoint input is what permits the single pass.
whys.b: R is the cause, not a side fact.

questions.prompt: Consider the size of IPv4 subnets.
questions.explanation: Host bits = 32 - prefix length; addresses = 2 to the power of host bits.

whys.a: The 32-bit width alone does not give 256; the 8 host bits left by /24 do.
whys.b: Right: both are true, but the size follows from the 8 remaining host bits, so the address width is not the explanation by itself.

questions.prompt: Brian Kernighan's popcount loop repeats n = n & (n - 1) until n is zero.
questions.explanation: Each loop iteration removes one set bit, so the loop runs once per 1 bit.
questions.assertion: The expression n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit of n.
questions.reason: Subtracting 1 flips every bit of n.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Right: A is true, but subtracting 1 flips only the lowest set bit and the zeros below it, not every bit; R is false.

questions.explanation: a ^ a = 0 is what cancels the paired values in Single Number and Missing Number.
questions.assertion: For any integer a, a ^ a equals a.
questions.reason: For any integer a, a ^ 0 equals a.

whys.a: A is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.d: Right: a ^ a is 0, so A is false, while R is true.

questions.prompt: Match each interval problem with its standard technique.
questions.explanation: Sorting by start fits merging; a heap of end times tracks rooms in use; earliest-end-first is the greedy for activity selection; an ordered map checks neighbours in O(log n); the sorted input lets Insert Interval run in one O(n) pass.

left.text: Calendar booking: does a new event collide?
Insert one interval into a sorted disjoint list

right.text: Sort by end time, pick greedily
Ordered map with floor and ceiling lookups
Min-heap of end times (or sweep line)

questions.prompt: Complete the facts about a /27 IPv4 subnet.
questions.explanation: 27 network bits leave 5 host bits: 2^5 = 32 addresses, 30 usable. The last octet mask is 11100000 = 224. A /26 would give 64 and 62.
questions.text: A /27 has mask 255.255.255.{1}, {2} total addresses and {3} usable hosts.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which XOR facts are correct?
questions.explanation: XOR is associative and commutative, which is why the order of elements does not matter. Swapping without a temp is a party trick, not production code.

options.why: Correct: each bit is identical, so every result bit is 0.
Correct: XOR with zero leaves every bit unchanged.

options.text: a ^ b == a + b for all non-negative a and b.
options.why: False: 1 ^ 1 = 0 but 1 + 1 = 2; they agree only when no bit position is set in both.

options.text: XOR of all elements returns the value that appears once if every other value appears exactly twice.
options.why: Correct: pairs cancel to 0 and the single value remains.

questions.prompt: Write pseudocode for in_subnet(ip, network, prefix_len): true when the 32-bit unsigned IPv4 address ip belongs to the CIDR block network/prefix_len. Use bit operations and handle prefix_len = 0.
questions.explanation: The mask keeps the network bits and zeroes the host bits, so both sides are compared on the network part only. The zero-length guard matters in languages where shifting by 32 does nothing. An XOR-and-shift form works too.

checks.label: applies the mask with a bitwise AND
compares the masked values for equality

questions.prompt: Complete the recurrence that counts the set bits of every number from 0 to n in O(n).
questions.explanation: This is LeetCode 338 (Counting Bits). The answer for i reuses an already computed smaller number, so it is a DP over bits; i & (i - 1) works too: bits[i] = bits[i & (i - 1)] + 1.
questions.text: With bits[0] = {1}, use bits[i] = bits[i {2} 1] + (i {3} 1): drop the lowest bit, then add it back if it was set.
